title: Exact pair density wave in topological moire flat bands and universal superfluid stiffness
summary: Pair-density waves (PDWs) are unconventional superconducting states beyond the BCS paradigm, but identifying them unambiguously in microscopic lattice models is generally challenging due to various competing orders. In particular, an exact realization of PDW in interacting models with topological bands remains elusive. Here we construct an interacting model on a twisted bilayer checkerboard lattice (TBCB) featuring topological flat bands, and rigorously show that an exact PDW ground state can be induced by quantum geometric nesting (QGN), owing to its momentum-space nonsymmorphic symmetry. We further prove that the superfluid stiffness of any nondegenerate QGN superconductor (including the PDW studied here and uniform superconductor) obeys the universal relation $D_s=2N_{\rm flat}ν(1-ν)m_{\rm pair}^{-1}$, where $N_{\rm flat}$, $ν$, and $m_{\rm pair}$ are the number of flat bands, flat band filling, and the two-particle effective mass, respectively. Our results reveal a rich interplay among PDW order, quantum geometry, and band topology.

AI.tldr: The authors construct an interacting model on a twisted bilayer checkerboard lattice with topological flat bands and rigorously demonstrate an exact pair-density-wave (PDW) ground state driven by quantum geometric nesting (QGN) enabled by a momentum-space nonsymmorphic symmetry. They also prove a universal formula for the superfluid stiffness of any nondegenerate QGN superconductor: D_s = 2 N_flat ν(1−ν) m_pair^{-1}.
AI.method: Analytic construction and rigorous proof: design of an interacting microscopic model on a twisted bilayer checkerboard lattice (TBCB) with topological flat bands, identification of quantum geometric nesting due to momentum-space nonsymmorphic symmetry, and derivation of an exact PDW ground state and a universal relation for superfluid stiffness.

title: Supercurrent detection and manipulation of topological phase transitions in Shiba-Majorana hybrid systems
summary: The non-Abelian statistics of Majorana zero modes has inspired numerous proposals for their detection and manipulation in topological superconductors. Implementations based on magnetic adatoms deposited on superconductors draw particular attention due to their capabilities for precise atomic manipulation and the control over disorder. Here, we propose a scheme for detecting changes in the ground state parity of a topologically non-trivial adatom system by passing supercurrent through their low-energy modes. We unravel characteristic discontinuities in the critical current driven by zero-energy level crossings. We apply these findings to a setup where the Majorana coupling is mediated by a single control magnetic adatom hosting a Yu-Shiba-Rusinov state, and test the robustness of our results against finite temperatures and different tunneling regimes. Our findings introduce a non-invasive approach for reading out and controlling the ground state parity of Majorana states in Shiba-Majorana hybrid systems.

AI.tldr: Proposes a non-invasive scheme to read out and control the fermion parity of Majorana states in magnetic-adatom / superconductor hybrids by passing supercurrent through their low-energy modes; predicts characteristic discontinuities in the critical Josephson current at zero-energy level crossings and demonstrates the effect for a setup where a single control magnetic adatom (hosting a Yu–Shiba–Rusinov state) mediates Majorana coupling, with robustness checked against finite temperature and different tunneling regimes.
AI.method: Theoretical proposal and modeling of Josephson transport through low-energy Shiba–Majorana modes: analyze how zero-energy level crossings alter the critical supercurrent (producing discontinuities) and apply the analysis to a concrete geometry where Majorana coupling is mediated by a single magnetic adatom hosting a YSR state; test effects of finite temperature and varying tunneling regimes to assess robustness.

title: Strain-driven orbital-selective reconstruction and bicollinear-to-stripe evolution in FeTe
summary: FeTe, as a representative parent material among iron-based superconductors, provides an ideal platform for exploring the interplay among orbital-selective correlations, magnetism, and unconventional superconductivity. However, a unified picture of the correlated electronic structure and magnetism of FeTe under strain remains to be fully clarified. Here, combining density functional theory plus dynamical mean-field theory and Heisenberg model analysis, we uncover an orbital-selective reconstruction of the correlated electronic structure and reveal a strain-driven trajectory from bicollinear to stripe antiferromagnetism (AFM) via an intermediate competing staggered $n$-mer AFM regime in FeTe. Moderate strain gives rise to a regime where more coherent quasiparticles coexist with suppressed local moments. Further strain drives FeTe into an incoherent correlated regime with robust local moments and Fe-$3d_{z^2}$-dominated low-energy states. These results establish a strain-driven trajectory across distinct magnetic and correlated electronic states in FeTe.

AI.tldr: DFT+DMFT combined with Heisenberg-model analysis shows that tensile strain in FeTe drives an orbital‑selective reconstruction of its correlated electronic structure and a magnetic trajectory from bicollinear AFM → intermediate staggered n‑mer AFM → stripe AFM. Moderate strain produces coexisting more coherent quasiparticles and suppressed local moments; stronger strain yields an incoherent correlated state with robust local moments and Fe‑3d_{z^2} dominated low‑energy states.
AI.method: First‑principles electronic structure with density functional theory plus dynamical mean‑field theory (DFT+DMFT), supplemented by mapping to a Heisenberg model to analyze magnetic phase competition under strain.

title: Stabilization of Interband Phase Solitons in Two-Band Noncentrosymmetric Superconducting Rings
comment: 6 pages of the main text with 4 figures and the supplemental material. Comments are welcome
summary: Two-band superconductors maintain a relative interband phase which can carry winding soliton excitations in a superconducting ring, supported by independent winding numbers in the two bands. In rings of superconductors obeying the inversion symmetry the interband phase solitons are metastable states, separated from the uniform ground state by the energy of screening currents. In this work we find that, breaking the inversion symmetry strongly enough, one can make the soliton a true ground state. In that case, a magneto-electric coupling, absent in centrosymmetric materials, contributes critically above a certain threshold, a relevant, free-energy term, odd with respect to the winding number, which biases the energy balance in favor of a particular winding sign. Once the bias outweighs the energy cost that originally made the soliton metastable, a phase soliton with a finite winding number becomes the ground state, with chirality set by the applied field. In current--flux measurements performed in equilibrium states, the effect is demonstrated by field-odd soliton branches, that replace the metastable ones existing in mesoscopic rings, built by two-component superconductors, realizing a magneto-electric analog of the Little--Parks fluxoid-branch physics in the interband relative-phase sector.

AI.tldr: Breaking inversion symmetry in two-band superconducting rings can make interband phase solitons (relative-phase windings) into true ground states. A magneto-electric coupling, absent in centrosymmetric systems and odd in winding number, biases chirality and, above a threshold, overcomes screening-current energy costs so that field-selected soliton branches replace metastable ones; this produces field-odd soliton branches observable in equilibrium current–flux measurements, analogous to Little–Parks fluxoid branches but in the interband phase sector.
AI.method: Analytical and/or phenomenological free-energy analysis of two-component superconducting rings with broken inversion symmetry, identifying a magneto-electric coupling term odd in winding number and computing energy balance between screening currents and interband phase winding to determine ground-state transitions and current–flux signatures.

title: Quantized Transport through a Supermoiré Chern Mosaic
summary: Magic-angle helical trilayer graphene---three graphene layers sequentially twisted in the same direction by $\sim1.8^\circ$---relaxes into a mosaic of domains that, at zero field, carry opposite valley-resolved Chern numbers, with boundaries hosting a network of gapless conducting modes. Charge transport through this network depends sensitively on how the modes connect and scatter, making well-quantized transport unlikely. Contrary to this expectation, we observe a field-induced Chern gap with Chern number $C=-6$ emanating from charge neutrality; in this gap, the Hall resistance is quantized to within $2\%$ of the expected value, $-h/6e^2$, at 4.6 K. We explain this behavior using both Hofstadter and orbital Zeeman calculations, which show that a moderate magnetic field drives a valley-selective topological transition. Above the transition, the total Chern number of the occupied states in each spin-valley flavor becomes identical across neighboring domains, and the domain-wall modes can become gapped. Though the central valence-band Chern numbers still differ between the two domain types, the observed quantized transport attests to a global gap.

AI.tldr: Magic-angle helical trilayer graphene (HTG) exhibits a field-induced global Chern gap at charge neutrality with Chern number C = -6 and Hall resistance quantized to ≈ -h/6e^2 at 4.6 K, despite an underlying mosaic of domains with opposite valley-resolved Chern numbers. A moderate magnetic field drives a valley-selective topological transition that aligns occupied-state Chern numbers across neighboring domains and gaps the domain-wall modes, producing the observed quantized transport.
AI.method: Combined experimental low-temperature magnetotransport (Hall resistance) measurements on magic-angle helical trilayer graphene and theoretical modeling using Hofstadter-butterfly band-structure calculations together with orbital Zeeman effect analysis to demonstrate a valley-selective topological transition.

title: High-Temperature Superconductivity of the Fe-Se-H compound
summary: Using an EPR spectrometer, the dependences of microwave power absorption on magnetic field up to 6000 Oe were measured at temperatures of 3.6-25 K and 295 K in a powdered compound Fe-Se-H, obtained by thermal diffusion of hydrogen into a FeSe single crystal with a critical temperature of 8 K. The shape of the dependences and the analysis of the measurement results confirm the superconductivity of the Fe-Se-H compound at normal pressure, both at temperatures of 3.6-25 K and at 295 K, i.e., at room temperature.

AI.tldr: EPR measurements of microwave power absorption in powdered Fe–Se–H (hydrogenated FeSe) show field-dependent signals at 3.6–25 K and at 295 K that the authors interpret as evidence of superconductivity at ambient pressure, including a claim of superconductivity at room temperature. The parent FeSe crystal had Tc = 8 K prior to hydrogen diffusion.
AI.method: Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy measuring microwave power absorption as a function of applied magnetic field (up to 6000 Oe) on powdered Fe–Se–H samples, at temperatures 3.6–25 K and 295 K; analysis of the shape of field-dependent absorption traces used to infer superconductivity.
specific_terms: microwave power absorption vs magnetic field (≤6000 Oe)

title: Hidden Frustration in Collinear Altermagnets: Pairing Vortices and Equilibrium Spin Current Loops
summary: We show that a magnet can remain perfectly collinear while its quantum vacuum circulates. In a centrosymmetric altermagnet, a symmetry-allowed locally staggered Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya coupling imprints a gauge-irremovable vortex-antivortex pair into the anomalous magnon pair correlations at high-symmetry points in momentum space. In real space, these hidden vortices produce an antiferrochiral array of equilibrium spin currents circulating oppositely around neighboring plaquettes. Gauge-irremovable frustration therefore survives despite classical collinearity: it exists entirely in the quantum correlations. Our results show that complex pairing, gauge-invariant fluxes, and equilibrium loop currents - structures encountered across electronic flux phases, spin liquids, and frustrated quantum magnets - can be encoded in the squeezed vacuum of a collinear magnet.

AI.tldr: In a centrosymmetric altermagnet, a symmetry-allowed locally staggered Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya coupling imprints a gauge‑irremovable vortex–antivortex pair into anomalous magnon pair correlations (the squeezed magnon vacuum) at high‑symmetry momenta. In real space this manifests as an antiferrochiral array of equilibrium spin currents circulating oppositely on neighboring plaquettes—i.e., gauge‑invariant loop currents and frustration encoded entirely in quantum correlations despite classical collinearity.
AI.method: Theoretical symmetry and many‑body analysis of magnon pair correlations in a centrosymmetric altermagnet with a locally staggered Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya coupling; identification of vortex–antivortex textures in momentum‑space anomalous correlators and mapping to real‑space equilibrium spin currents in the squeezed magnon vacuum.

title: How quantum is quantum geometry?
summary: The quantum geometric tensor - the Berry curvature together with the quantum metric - now underlies a long list of observables, from the anomalous Hall effect to the superfluid weight of a flat band. We ask which of these observables actually require quantum mechanics. To answer this question, we study a purely classical system: a point particle carrying a classical magnetic moment $\boldsymbol{\ell}$ that precesses in a momentum-dependent magnetic field $\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{p})$. Within Hamiltonian classical mechanics, the component of $\boldsymbol{\ell}$ along the field reproduces the Berry-curvature phenomena, while its precessing transverse component reproduces the quantum-metric phenomena. The particle acquires a position spread whose second moment is the metric, an orbital magnetic moment, and - most strikingly - an inertial mass generated by a position-dependent force, and with it a nonzero Drude weight in a system that is nominally dispersionless.

AI.tldr: A purely classical model—a point particle carrying a classical magnetic moment ℓ that precesses in a momentum-dependent field B(p)—reproduces signatures of the quantum geometric tensor: the ℓ-component along B yields Berry-curvature phenomena, and the transverse precessing component yields quantum-metric phenomena. The model predicts a position spread whose second moment equals the metric, an orbital magnetic moment, and an emergent inertial mass (hence a nonzero Drude weight) even for an otherwise dispersionless system.
AI.method: Hamiltonian classical-mechanics analysis of a point particle with a classical magnetic moment in a momentum-dependent magnetic field B(p); decomposition of ℓ into longitudinal (along B) and transverse (precessing) components and calculation of resulting position moments, orbital moment, inertial mass and transport (Drude) response.

title: Topologically protected perfect crossed Andreev reflection in flux-engineered quantum wire junctions
summary: Generating non-locally entangled electron pairs via Cooper-pair splitting is vital for solid-state quantum information processing. However, isolating the underlying crossed Andreev reflection (CAR) is challenging due to competing transport processes like electron tunneling (ET) and local Andreev reflection (AR). Here, we propose a flux-tunable four-terminal normal metal-superconductor junction that achieves deterministic, 100\% efficient CAR. We demonstrate that at exactly half a magnetic flux quantum ($φ=π$), exact destructive Aharonov-Bohm and Peierls interferences structurally forbid ET and AR respectively. By tuning the central junction hopping, electron reflection is also suppressed to zero. Using the Cauchy argument principle, we prove that this suppression manifests as a quantized topological winding number, guaranteeing a topologically protected unit CAR probability. We establish that this regime is characterized by a strictly positive cross-correlation shot noise, providing an unambiguous experimental signature of Cooper-pair splitting. Furthermore, this perfect CAR is nearly broadband within the superconducting gap and remarkably robust against structural disorder, offering a highly resilient architecture for deterministic nonlocal entanglement generation.

AI.tldr: Proposes a flux-tunable four-terminal normal–superconductor device that achieves deterministic, 100% crossed Andreev reflection (Cooper-pair splitting) at half a flux quantum (φ=π). ET and AR are cancelled by Aharonov–Bohm and Peierls interference while electron reflection is nulled by tuning the central hopping; a Cauchy-argument-principle-based topological winding number guarantees unit CAR, with a positive cross-correlation shot-noise signature and robustness against disorder across much of the superconducting gap.
AI.method: Analytical and theoretical transport analysis of a flux-threaded four-terminal NS junction using interference arguments (Aharonov–Bohm and Peierls phases), tuning of central junction hopping, and a topological proof based on the Cauchy argument principle; shot-noise (cross-correlation) calculations to identify experimental signatures and disorder robustness checks.

title: Majorana signatures in an asymmetrically coupled quantum dot--topological superconducting nanowire junction
summary: We present a theoretical study of the quantum transport through a nanoscale system in which a central quantum dot (QD) is coupled asymmetrically to normal leads and to two Majorana bound states (MBSs) localized at the ends of a topological superconducting nanowire threaded by a tunable magnetic flux. The effects of the leads--QD coupling asymmetry parameter $α$ and the bias voltage asymmetry parameter $q$ on the system's linear conductance are considered for the case of unhybridized and hybridized MBSs. In the zero-temperature limit, for unhybridized MBSs the system's linear conductance is finite only when the magnetic flux phase $φ= (2n+1)π$ ($n\in\mathbb{Z}$) and it scales as $\mathcal{G}=2qαe^2/[h(α+1)]$, while for hybridized MBSs it presents a complicated dependence on the system's parameters. At finite temperature, for unhybridized MBSs, the system's linear conductance oscillates as a function of the magnetic flux phase $φ$ with a period of $2π$, and the position of the linear conductance maxima can be shifted from $φ=2nπ$ to $φ=(2n+1)π$ by simply varying the value of the bias voltage asymmetry parameter $q$. For hybridized MBSs, the conductance exhibits a similar behavior when the energy level of the central QD, $\varepsilon_d$, is tuned at the leads' Fermi level ($\varepsilon_d=\varepsilon_F$), although when $\varepsilon_d\neq\varepsilon_F$ the oscillation period changes to $4π$, and the position of the linear conductance maxima depends on the actual value of $\varepsilon_d$ and other parameters in the system. Our results highlight the experimental importance of the leads-QD and bias voltage asymmetry parameters, which are often present in realistic experimental setups, and can strongly affect the identification and observation of MBSs transport signatures.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes linear conductance through a nanoscale device consisting of an asymmetric quantum dot coupled to normal leads and two Majorana bound states at the ends of a topological superconducting nanowire pierced by a tunable magnetic flux. It shows that lead–QD coupling asymmetry (α) and bias asymmetry (q) strongly modify conductance signatures: for unhybridized MBSs at zero temperature conductance is nonzero only at flux phase φ=(2n+1)π with G=2qαe^2/[h(α+1)], while at finite T the conductance oscillates with period 2π and maxima shift with q. For hybridized MBSs the dependence is more complex: when ε_d=ε_F behavior resembles the unhybridized case, but for ε_d≠ε_F the oscillation period becomes 4π and peak positions depend on ε_d and other parameters. The study highlights that realistic asymmetries can mask or shift expected MBS transport signatures.
AI.method: Theoretical quantum-transport analysis of linear conductance as a function of system parameters (lead–QD coupling asymmetry α, bias asymmetry q, magnetic flux phase φ, QD level ε_d, and MBS hybridization), evaluated in zero-temperature and finite-temperature limits.
specific_terms: QD level ε_d and Fermi level ε_F
linear conductance G (G=2qαe^2/[h(α+1)] for unhybridized MBSs at φ=(2n+1)π)

title: Occupation-Driven Josephson Diode in a Symmetric Junction
summary: We propose a Josephson diode mechanism in which nonreciprocity arises not from a conventional asymmetric Andreev spectrum but from nonequilibrium occupation of the current-carrying states engineered by attached reservoirs. We realize this mechanism in a double-quantum-dot junction, where a phase-textured nonlocal reservoir acts as a quantum Zeno selector: rapid dissipation freezes out the bright state directly coupled to the jump operator $L$, while preserving an orthogonal dark Andreev channel whose supercurrent remains comparable to that of the lossless junction. In the infinite-gap limit, the steady-state current factorizes as $I_{\rm ss}=I_A P_γ$, so that even when the Andreev current $I_A$ is strictly reciprocal, the phase asymmetry of $P_γ$ alone can produce a Josephson diode effect through reservoir engineering. We further show that local Coulomb repulsion can drive the system toward a nearly ideal diode regime via a dark-pair resonance. Using Keldysh-Lindblad calculations, we demonstrate that our results remain robust for realistic junctions with a finite superconducting gap and dissipation.

AI.tldr: Proposal of a Josephson-diode mechanism driven by nonequilibrium occupation engineered via attached reservoirs in a double-quantum-dot junction: a phase-textured nonlocal reservoir uses a quantum-Zeno-like dissipation to freeze a 'bright' Andreev channel while preserving a 'dark' channel, producing nonreciprocal steady-state supercurrent even when the intrinsic Andreev spectrum is reciprocal. Coulomb repulsion can enhance diode behavior via a dark-pair resonance; results are supported by Keldysh–Lindblad calculations including finite-gap and dissipation effects.
AI.method: Theoretical modeling of a double-quantum-dot Josephson junction with reservoir engineering; analytic infinite-gap limit yielding I_ss = I_A P_γ factorization; open-system nonequilibrium calculations using a Keldysh–Lindblad formalism to capture dissipation, the quantum-Zeno selection, and finite-gap effects.
specific_terms: quantum Zeno selector (dissipative dark/bright state screening)

title: Magnetic Communication with an Acoustically Actuated Magnetoelectric Resonator and a Quantum Diamond Magnetometer
summary: Wireless communication via propagating magnetic fields is a communication modality that has recently garnered significant interest for short-to-medium range communication in conductive mediums, such as underwater and underground, where existing approaches utilizing electric fields are highly inefficient. Typical implementations of magnetic communication make use of loop antennas as both the transmitter and receiver, with the sensitivity and frequency response scaling with and inversely with the loop cross-sectional area, respectively. Here, we explore an alternative hybrid magnetic communication system consisting of an highly radiation efficient and compact acoustically actuated magnetoelectric resonator as the transmitter, and a highly sensitive micrometer scale quantum magnetometer based on nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond as the receiver, with their core properties unconstrained by size. We demonstrate amplitude and phase-encoded transmission and reception of AC magnetic fields at $f_{\mathrm{AC}}$ = 20 kHz, achieving a sensitivity of 50 pT/$\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$ and 1.2 mrad/$\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$, respectively. This work establishes the use of hybrid magnetoelectric resonator and quantum diamond magnetometer communication system as a viable alternative to existing loop-based approaches.

AI.tldr: Demonstrates a hybrid magnetic wireless link using an acoustically actuated magnetoelectric resonator transmitter and a nitrogen-vacancy (NV) diamond quantum magnetometer receiver, achieving amplitude- and phase-encoded AC magnetic communication at 20 kHz with measured sensitivities (50 pT/√Hz amplitude, 1.2 mrad/√Hz phase).
AI.method: Combine a compact, high-radiation-efficiency acoustically actuated magnetoelectric resonator as the transmitter with a micrometer-scale NV-center diamond quantum magnetometer as the receiver; implement amplitude and phase encoding of a 20 kHz AC magnetic signal and characterize receiver sensitivity.

title: Scalable, Simple, and Versatile Encapsulation of 2D Materials and Devices
summary: Air-sensitive 2D materials present a fundamental challenge for device integration. Encapsulation is often required to preserve intrinsic properties, yet conventional protection strategies often fail for thicker layers and complicate fabrication. Here, we demonstrate that electron-beam (e-beam) evaporated aluminum oxide ($\mathrm{AlO}_x$) serves as both an effective encapsulation layer and a platform for direct device fabrication. Unlike transfer-based approaches, this scalable method is compatible with thicker flakes and full device or wafer coverage. It requires no stacking procedures and enables contacts without post-encapsulation etching. Using rare-earth tritellurides ($\mathrm{RTe}_3$, R = La, Er), semimetallic $\mathrm{WTe}_2$, and superconducting $\mathrm{FeTe}_x\mathrm{Se}_{1-x}$, we show that $\mathrm{AlO}_x$ suppresses oxidation and preserves intrinsic optical and electronic properties. We establish substrate-dependent optimization of encapsulation across a range of flake thicknesses, demonstrate that ultrathin $\mathrm{AlO}_x$ preserves $\mathrm{WTe}_2$'s plasmonic response and maintains superconducting performance in $\mathrm{FeTe}_x\mathrm{Se}_{1-x}$. Thus we overcome the longstanding tradeoff between encapsulation and straightforward device fabrication in fragile quantum materials.

AI.tldr: Electron-beam evaporated aluminum oxide (AlO_x) is demonstrated as a scalable, direct- fabrication-compatible encapsulation that suppresses oxidation and preserves intrinsic optical and electronic properties of air-sensitive 2D and quasi-2D quantum materials (RTe_3, WTe_2, FeTe_xSe_{1-x}), working across a range of flake thicknesses and enabling contacts without post-encapsulation etching.
AI.method: Direct e-beam evaporation of AlO_x as an encapsulation layer applied to flakes on substrate, with substrate-dependent optimization of layer thickness and demonstration of device compatibility (contacting and wafer-scale coverage) without transfer or etching steps.

title: Statistical Disorder in MBE-Grown AlGaAs/GaAs Superlattices for Quantum Bragg Mirrors using Synchrotron X-ray Diffraction
summary: AlGaAs/GaAs superlattices grown by Molecular Beam Epitaxy (MBE) are foundational for advanced optoelectronic devices, including Quantum Bragg Mirror (QBM) infrared detectors. The performance of these devices critically depends on achieving near-perfect periodicity and abrupt interfaces, however, intrinsic statistical fluctuations during MBE growth introduce nanoscale structural disorder that can degrade device efficiency. In this study, we present a comprehensive methodology for quantifying this disorder in a 203-layer QBM device. High-resolution structural characterization was performed using high-energy (25 keV) synchrotron X-ray diffraction. By coupling a recursive dynamical diffraction formalism with an ensemble simulated annealing refinement, we extracted statistically robust, layer-by-layer thickness profiles. Our analysis reveals highly systematic, material-specific deviations from the nominal design: all AlGaAs barrier layers were consistently thinner than nominal by 0.3-0.6 nm. Furthermore, the sequential thickness profile successfully identified a significant 35 nm deficit in the final macroscopic top contact layer and a 40 nm deficit in the first GaAs layer. Achieving a statistical precision of about 0.2 to 0.6 nm (approximately 1-2 atomic monolayers), this non-destructive diagnostic approach provides directly actionable feedback for MBE flux calibration protocols.

AI.tldr: Non-destructive, high-precision quantification of nanoscale thickness disorder in a 203-layer AlGaAs/GaAs Quantum Bragg Mirror grown by MBE: 25 keV synchrotron XRD combined with recursive dynamical diffraction and ensemble simulated annealing yields layer-by-layer thickness profiles with ~0.2–0.6 nm precision, revealing systematic AlGaAs barrier thinning (0.3–0.6 nm) and large thickness deficits in the top contact (−35 nm) and first GaAs layer (−40 nm).
AI.method: High-energy (25 keV) synchrotron X-ray diffraction measured diffraction from the 203-layer superlattice; data were analyzed using a recursive dynamical diffraction formalism coupled to an ensemble simulated annealing refinement to extract statistically robust, layer-by-layer thickness profiles non-destructively.

title: Optical spectroscopy of composite fermion edge states in the fractional quantum Hall effect
summary: We show that edge states in fractional quantum Hall effect samples can be selectively probed and excited with sub-terahertz optical spectroscopy. Using the composite fermion (CF) mean-field framework, which maps the strongly correlated fractional quantum Hall problem onto an effective integer quantum Hall problem, we calculate the absorbance spectrum for the Jain sequence of filling fractions including both bulk and edge states. The CF edge-state absorption peaks appear in the millimeter-wave to sub-terahertz range, e.g., 60-500 GHz at B = 10 T in GaAs, i.e. they are blueshifted with respect to the bulk CF cyclotron frequency but are well below the integer quantum Hall cyclotron frequency scale at the same magnetic fields. The number of resolved peaks in each series of the absorption spectrum counts the filled Lambda-levels and fingerprints the fraction. Inversion symmetry breaking near the edge activates optical transitions forbidden in the bulk and enables second-order nonlinear processes in electric-dipole approximation. The absolute frequency scale of the spectrum is set by the CF effective mass, which is generated entirely by electron-electron interactions, so the absorption spectrum provides a direct optical probe of this interaction-induced mass.

AI.tldr: Sub‑terahertz (millimeter-wave) optical spectroscopy can selectively probe edge states in fractional quantum Hall samples. Using the composite‑fermion mean‑field mapping for the Jain sequence, the calculated absorbance shows edge CF peaks (e.g. 60–500 GHz at B=10 T in GaAs) whose number counts filled Λ‑levels; inversion‑symmetry breaking at the edge activates optically forbidden transitions and enables second‑order nonlinear responses. The overall frequency scale is set by the interaction‑generated composite‑fermion effective mass, so the spectrum directly probes that mass.
AI.method: Composite‑fermion mean‑field mapping of the fractional quantum Hall problem onto an effective integer quantum Hall problem; calculation of absorbance spectra for the Jain sequence including both bulk and edge contributions, with attention to symmetry breaking near edges and electric‑dipole processes (including second‑order nonlinearities).
specific_terms: edge‑state absorption peaks (60–500 GHz at B=10 T in GaAs)

title: Observation of dodecagonal replica bands in 30$^{\circ}$-twisted bilayer WSe$_2$
summary: Twisted bilayers of two-dimensional (2D) transition metal dichalcogenides are promising systems for achieving tunable quasicrystalline orders with emergent properties. The underpinning electronic structure and scattering processes in 2D quasicrystals with multiorbital dodecagonal replica bands have so far not been determined. Here, we utilize angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) with micrometer spatial resolution to directly observe replica bands in 30$^{\circ}$-twisted bilayer WSe$_2$. The symmetry and intensity distribution of the observed replicas are explained by interlayer Umklapp scattering from bottom to top WSe$_2$ layers. Our spectral function measurements are consistent with the presence of a van Hove singularity adjacent to the $\mathrm{K}$-valleys, which underlines the possibility of inducing electronic reconstructions in bilayers with a large interlayer twist angle.

AI.tldr: Micro‑ARPES directly reveals dodecagonal replica bands in 30° twisted bilayer WSe2; their symmetry and intensity are explained by interlayer Umklapp scattering, and the spectral function shows a van Hove singularity near the K valleys implying possible electronic reconstruction at large twist angles.
AI.method: Micrometer-resolved angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (micro-ARPES) measurements of the spectral function combined with analysis of symmetry and intensity distributions to identify interlayer Umklapp scattering as the origin of observed replica bands.

title: Switchable giant room-temperature nonlinear Hall effect in Bilayer Graphene
summary: Utilizing quantum second-order nonlinear transport for practical junction-free devices require materials with large and tunable nonlinearites at room temperature -- a current materials platform challenge. Here, we report the nonlinear Hall effect (NLHE) in double-ionic gated bilayer graphene devices that enable unusually strong inversion breaking. We observe NLHE that are readily switchable (on, off, and sign reversed) with second order nonlinear susceptibilities $χ^{(2)}_{yxx}$ that reaches giant room-temperature values of $3\,10^{-3}\,μ\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{S/V}$, comparable to values commonly observed at low temperature in WTe$_2$ or in graphene-based moiré superlattices, and three-to-four orders of magnitude larger than values reported in material systems recently employed in search of a room-temperature NLHE. Our devices produce corresponding THz voltage responsivities $\simeq 4\,10^{4}\,\mathrm{V/W}$, comparable to commercially available Schottky diodes. These are orders of magnitude better than for previously reported room-temperature NLHE devices rendering double-ionic gated bilayer graphene a choice platform for junction-free nonlinear technology.

AI.tldr: Double‑ionic gated bilayer graphene exhibits a giant, switchable room‑temperature nonlinear Hall effect (NLHE) via strong inversion‑symmetry breaking, with χ^{(2)}_{yxx} ≈ 3×10^{-3} μm·S/V and THz voltage responsivity ≈4×10^4 V/W — values comparable to low‑T WTe2 and to commercial Schottky diodes, making junction‑free nonlinear devices feasible.
AI.method: Fabrication and electrical/transport measurement of double‑ionic gated bilayer graphene devices to induce strong, tunable inversion‑symmetry breaking and characterize the second‑order nonlinear Hall response and THz voltage responsivity at room temperature.

title: Exceptional point induced by hyperbolicity in an electrostatic spherical shell
summary: Exceptional points (EPs) are non--Hermitian degeneracies at which both eigenvalues and eigenvectors coalesce, usually engineered through balanced gain and loss or non--reciprocity. In this work, we show that the radial electrostatic problem of an anisotropic core--shell nanoparticle realizes an EP without any of the alluded conditons. Written in the logarithmic radial coordinate, the problem is a Cauchy--Euler equation that maps onto a damped oscillator and, equivalently, onto a two-site Hatano--Nelson Hamiltonian, so that the non-Hermiticity is emulated in space rather than in time and the sole control parameter is the degree of dielectric anisotropy, $\varepsilon_t/\varepsilon_r$. The shell is passive, reciprocal, and lossless, yet it hosts an EP and a non--Hermitian phase transition governed by hyperbolicity alone. Beyond a hyperbolicity threshold the electric field inside the shell turns from monotonic decay into spatial oscillation, producing hotspots at intermediate radii which can be exploited to tailor fluorescence, strong coupling, sensing, or cloaking. More broadly, this establishes hyperbolic media as a platform to simulate non--Hermitian physics without gain, loss, or non--reciprocity.

AI.tldr: Anisotropic core–shell nanoparticles host an exceptional point (EP) and a non‑Hermitian phase transition without gain, loss, or non‑reciprocity: mapping the radial electrostatic problem (in a logarithmic radial coordinate) onto a Cauchy–Euler equation yields an equivalence to a damped oscillator and a two‑site Hatano–Nelson Hamiltonian. The single control parameter is dielectric anisotropy ε_t/ε_r; above a hyperbolicity threshold the shell’s field changes from monotonic decay to spatial oscillation, creating intermediate‑radius hotspots with applications in fluorescence, strong coupling, sensing, and cloaking.
AI.method: Analytical mapping of the radial electrostatic problem in an anisotropic core–shell nanoparticle using a logarithmic radial coordinate to transform the Cauchy–Euler equation into a damped oscillator and an equivalent two‑site Hatano–Nelson non‑Hermitian Hamiltonian, identifying an EP and hyperbolicity‑driven phase transition.

title: Hall effect in viscous flows of two-dimensional electrons in samples with edges of arbitrary roughness
summary: In ultra-clean conductors, fast inter-particle collisions can lead to the formation of a viscous electron fluid and realization of the hydrodynamic transport regime. Here we develop a theory of hydrodynamic magnetotransport of two-dimensional (2D) electrons in samples with low densities of defects and edges of arbitrary roughness. Within our model the roughness is described by a single parameter with the dimension of speed in the boundary conditions on sample edges. The electron-fluid flow profiles in long samples, as well as the corresponding longitudinal and Hall resistances, are calculated. The contribution to the Hall resistance associated with the relaxation processes exhibits a saturation in the limit of high magnetic field and a minimum as a function of the magnetic field for sufficiently rough edges. The minimum disappears as the edge roughness decreases or the sample width and bulk scattering by defects increase. These properties of the Hall resistance can serve as the signs to identify the hydrodynamic regime of electron transport in experiments and can be used to determine its parameters, in particular, the degree of edge roughness.

AI.tldr: Theory of hydrodynamic magnetotransport for 2D viscous electron fluids in long, ultra-clean samples with arbitrary edge roughness parameterized by a single speed-like boundary parameter. Calculated flow profiles and longitudinal/Hall resistances show that the Hall contribution from relaxation saturates at high magnetic field and can develop a field-dependent minimum for sufficiently rough edges; the minimum is suppressed by smoother edges, larger sample width, or increased bulk defect scattering. These features provide experimental diagnostics of hydrodynamic transport and edge roughness.
AI.method: Analytical/numerical solution of a hydrodynamic transport model for 2D electron fluids in long samples with boundary conditions that encode edge roughness through a single parameter (dimension of speed); computation of steady-state viscous flow profiles and resulting longitudinal and Hall resistances as functions of magnetic field, edge roughness, sample width, and bulk scattering.

title: Spin preservation in screw-symmetric molecules
summary: In electronic transport through long molecules, spin is expected to be preserved only when the dwell time is much shorter than the characteristic spin-mixing timescale $\hbar/Δ$, where $Δ$ is the magnitude of a spin-dependent potential, such as spin-orbit coupling. We show that, in molecules featuring discrete screw symmetry, spin preservation can be enhanced far beyond this timescale owing to strong spin separation in quasi-momentum. This spin fidelity in long molecules is consistent with chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS), suggesting spin-dependent transport in long, chiral molecules with amplified spin-splitting mechanisms. We provide analytical derivation of the enhanced spin preservation and test it on tight-binding models, which confirm that the effect gradually weakens when the screw symmetry is broken or changes from discrete to continuous. Furthermore, we perform transport simulations to show that a strong magnetoresistance trace of symmetry-protected spin fidelity emerges in a spin-valve setup with two magnetic leads, which we propose as an experimentally accessible signature.

AI.tldr: Discrete screw symmetry in long, chiral molecules can strongly enhance spin preservation well beyond the naive dwell-time vs. spin-mixing timescale ħ/Δ by producing strong spin separation in quasi-momentum. This provides a symmetry-protected mechanism consistent with CISS; tight-binding models and transport simulations show the effect weakens when screw symmetry is broken and predict a clear magnetoresistance signature in a spin-valve geometry with magnetic leads.
AI.method: Analytical derivation of symmetry-protected spin fidelity combined with numerical tight-binding calculations and quantum transport simulations (spin-valve setup) to test robustness under symmetry breaking and to extract an experimentally accessible magnetoresistance signature.

title: Magnon-induced phononic Chern insulator
summary: High-frequency artificial phononic crystals offer a low-loss platform compatible with on-chip integration, yet realizing Chern phononic phases at GHz frequencies remains challenging. Here, we propose a magnon-induced phononic Chern insulator in a honeycomb phononic crystal hybridized with ferromagnetic islands at the hexagon centers. A circularly polarized Kittel mode couples to the surrounding phonons with a phase winding, which breaks time-reversal symmetry and opens a full Chern gap. In the large-detuning regime, this mechanism leads to an effective Haldane-type phononic model with magnon-induced complex hopping. By tuning the magnon-phonon interaction, the full hybrid system accesses Chern phases with tunable Chern numbers |C|=1 and |C|=2. The predicted gaps can exceed realistic phonon and magnon linewidths, enabling their observation in GHz acoustic devices. Our work establishes chiral magnon--phonon hybridization as a route to magnetically reconfigurable topological phononics.

AI.tldr: Proposal for a magnon-induced phononic Chern insulator: a honeycomb phononic crystal with ferromagnetic islands hosts a circularly polarized Kittel magnon that hybridizes with phonons, breaking time-reversal symmetry and opening full Chern gaps at GHz frequencies. In the large-detuning limit the system maps to a Haldane-type phonon model with magnon-induced complex hopping, enabling tunable Chern phases |C|=1 and |C|=2 with gaps larger than realistic linewidths.
AI.method: Theoretical proposal and model-building: construct a hybrid system of a honeycomb phononic crystal with ferromagnetic islands at hexagon centers; derive magnon–phonon coupling (circularly polarized Kittel mode with phase winding) that breaks TRS; analyze large-detuning limit to obtain an effective Haldane-type phononic Hamiltonian with complex hopping; compute phase diagram showing tunable Chern numbers and estimate gap magnitudes relative to phonon/magnon linewidths.

title: Giant bulk photovoltaic effect driven by interfacial symmetry breaking in MoS2/Ta2NiSe5 heterostructures
summary: Van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures offer a versatile platform for engineering unconventional bulk photovoltaic (BPV) effect through interfacial symmetry breaking. However, the coexistence of multiple photophysical mechanisms, driven by structural complexity, spontaneous charge transfer, and strong interlayer coupling, often obscures the microscopic origin of the BPV response and hinders its rational optimization. Here, we demonstrate a pronounced BPV effect localized at the overlap region of a cross-bar MoS2/Ta2NiSe5 vdW heterostructure, where symmetry breaking induced by vertical stacking lifts the inversion center of MoS2. The orthogonal device geometry enables the independent probing of intralayer and interfacial photoresponse pathways, facilitating clear separation of competing mechanisms. Spontaneous interfacial charge transfer between MoS2 and Ta2NiSe5 further establishes a strong interlayer electronic coupling. By modulating the interlayer potential landscape through gate voltage and vertical electric fields, we achieve an optimized zero-bias photocurrent density of 247 A/cm2 and a BPV coefficient of 0.99 V-1. Supported by theoretical modelling, our results illustrate how minimalist device geometry can transform complex heterostructures into experimentally tractable platforms. This strategy paves the way for analyzing and optimizing interface-driven BPV effect, with implications for self-powered optoelectronics, broadband photodetection, and energy-harvesting nanodevices.

AI.tldr: Bulk photovoltaic (BPV) response is localized to the overlap of a cross‑bar MoS2/Ta2NiSe5 van der Waals heterostructure where vertical stacking breaks MoS2 inversion symmetry. Orthogonal device geometry separates intralayer vs interfacial photocurrent channels; spontaneous interfacial charge transfer creates strong interlayer coupling, and gate/vertical field tuning yields an optimized zero‑bias photocurrent density of 247 A/cm2 and a BPV coefficient of 0.99 V−1. Theoretical modelling supports the interpretation and points to a minimalist geometry for tractable interface‑driven BPV studies.
AI.method: Fabrication and measurement of an orthogonal (cross‑bar) MoS2/Ta2NiSe5 van der Waals heterostructure to spatially isolate overlap-region photoresponse; electrical gating and vertical electric‑field control to tune interlayer potential; spatially resolved photocurrent measurements to separate intralayer and interfacial mechanisms; theoretical modelling to interpret the BPV origin.

title: Terahertz anomalous Hall effect in magnetic Weyl semimetal Co$_3$Sn$_2$S$_2$
summary: Time-reversal-symmetry-broken Weyl semimetals are known to have at least two nodes in their electronic band structure, separated in momentum space and acting as sources and sinks of Berry curvature. This gives rise to a transverse Hall conductivity, known as the anomalous Hall effect (AHE), which, in the simplest two-node picture, is proportional to the momentum-space separation between the nodes in the zero frequency limit. In the recently discovered Weyl semimetal $\mathrm{Co_3Sn_2S_2}$, a giant AHE has been observed. However, experimental investigations in the low-energy regime, which directly probe quasiparticle excitations near the Weyl nodes, remain limited. Here, we present a systematic study of the intrinsic low-energy gyrotropic optical response of $\mathrm{Co_3Sn_2S_2}$ using terahertz spectroscopy combined with semianalytical calculations based on a physically intuitive effective model. Our results provide a robust and transparent explanation of the observed magnetooptical phenomena in terms of intrinsic gyrotropy arising from momentum-space separation of the Weyl nodes. Furthermore, quantitative comparison between experiment and theory places stringent constraints on the material parameters.

AI.tldr: Terahertz spectroscopy plus a semianalytical effective-model analysis shows that the giant low-frequency magneto‑optical response of Co3Sn2S2 is accounted for by intrinsic gyrotropy originating from momentum‑space separation of time‑reversal‑symmetry‑broken Weyl nodes; quantitative experiment–theory comparison constrains material parameters.
AI.method: Terahertz (low‑frequency) magneto‑optical spectroscopy combined with semianalytical calculations based on a physically motivated effective Weyl‑node model to compute intrinsic gyrotropic optical response.

title: Mobility Enhancement in Si/SiGe Quantum Well Enabled by a Buried Si Layer Trapping Oxygen Impurities
comment: Main 10 pages, Main 3 figures, Supporting 5 pages, Supporting 4 Figures
summary: Reducing disorder in undoped Si/SiGe field-effect heterostructures remains an important materials challenge for scalable quantum devices, particularly electron spin qubits. Background impurities such as oxygen have been identified as mobility-limiting, yet practical heterostructure-design strategies for suppressing their incorporation remain underexplored, and their influence across different transport regimes is not fully established. Here, we demonstrate a simple route to oxygen reduction and mobility enhancement in Si/SiGe quantum-well heterostructures grown by reduced-pressure chemical vapor deposition (RP-CVD) on 200 mm Si(100) substrates through the introduction of a thin, electrically passive buried Si layer within the lower SiGe barrier. Secondary-ion mass spectrometry shows that the buried Si layer reproducibly reduces the oxygen background in the subsequently grown SiGe by approximately a factor of five, without modifying the active quantum-well region. Density- and temperature-dependent magnetotransport measurements further show that this reduction increases the electron mobility, while leaving the percolation density and density-dependent mobility scaling largely unchanged. Upon cooling to 0.3 K, both high- and low-oxygen devices exhibit similar density-dependent fractional mobility enhancements, indicating that the reduced oxygen background improves momentum relaxation without substantially altering the dominant low-density disorder landscape. These results establish the buried Si layer as a straightforward and process-compatible heterostructure-design element for reducing oxygen incorporation and improving transport in 200 mm CVD-grown Si/SiGe quantum-device materials.

AI.tldr: Adding a thin, electrically passive buried Si layer inside the lower SiGe barrier during RP-CVD growth on 200 mm Si(100) substrates reduces oxygen incorporation in the overgrown SiGe by ≈5× and increases electron mobility in Si/SiGe quantum wells, while leaving percolation density and low-density disorder scaling largely unchanged; the approach is process-compatible for quantum-device materials.
AI.method: Materials-design and experimental characterization: insertion of a thin buried Si layer during reduced-pressure chemical vapor deposition (RP-CVD) growth of Si/SiGe quantum-well heterostructures on 200 mm Si(100) wafers, quantified by secondary-ion mass spectrometry (SIMS), and assessed via density- and temperature-dependent magnetotransport measurements down to 0.3 K.

title: Trapping $e/4$ quasiparticles in bilayer graphene
summary: Measuring the charge of the quasiparticles hosted by even-denominator fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states is essential to identify the topology of their ground state. Here, we use a gate-defined antidot in bilayer graphene, with an additional gate to control only the antidot potential, to measure the charge of the quasiparticles trapped around it in even-denominator FQH states. We observe a localized charge of $e/4$ at $ν=-5/2$, $-1/2$, and $3/2$, consistent with the minimal excitation expected for leading candidate even-denominator ground states, and $e/3$ at the hole-conjugate state $ν=2/3$. We further show that increasing the coupling between the antidot-bound states and extended edge states drives a crossover between two regimes, characterized by the minimal-excitation gate-voltage period and approximately twice that period, respectively. We discuss two possible explanations for this crossover: quasiparticle bunching and a crossover between distinct antidot transport regimes. Our results, together with previous observations of the daughter states, show that the even-denominator FQH states in bilayer graphene are compatible with a non-Abelian ground state, and that their quasiparticles can be localized around a quantum Hall antidot, a necessary ingredient for topological quantum computation.

AI.tldr: Gate-defined antidot spectroscopy in bilayer graphene reveals localized quasiparticle charge e/4 at even-denominator FQH states ν = −5/2, −1/2, 3/2 (and e/3 at ν = 2/3). Increasing coupling between antidot-bound and edge states produces a crossover in gate-voltage periodicity (minimal period → ≈2× period), attributed either to quasiparticle bunching or distinct antidot transport regimes. Results support compatibility of bilayer-graphene even-denominator states with a non‑Abelian ground state and demonstrate localized quasiparticles around an antidot—a prerequisite for topological qubit schemes.
AI.method: Device-scale gate-defined antidot in bilayer graphene with an independent antidot-control gate; detection of trapped quasiparticle charge via periodic gate-voltage signatures as coupling to extended edge states is tuned (antidot–edge coupling control).

title: Band's Geometry Origin of Quantum Spin Transport Phenomena
summary: We develop a geometric description of spin-dependent transport based on the local geometric structure of electronic bands and the Fermi surfaces. For quasi-two-dimensional systems, we show that hyperbolic regions of constant-energy surfaces generate a geometrical contribution to the Fermi velocity that couples naturally to electron spin and produces a spin-current response. We further show that, in the presence of time-reversal symmetry, the algebra of spin operators can be related to the exterior algebra of the band's tangent space, providing an additional geometric interpretation of spin in momentum space. This framework motivates a symplectic description of spin-separated transport on Fermi surfaces and its extension to three-dimensional band manifolds through contact geometry. Our results establish a direct connection between Fermi-surface geometry and intrinsic spin transport.

AI.tldr: A geometric formalism is developed that ties local Fermi-surface and band tangent-space geometry (notably hyperbolic constant-energy regions) to intrinsic spin-current responses; under time-reversal symmetry the spin operator algebra maps to the exterior algebra of the band tangent space, and spin-separated transport is formulated via symplectic (2D) and contact (3D) geometry.
AI.method: Construct a momentum-space geometric description: analyze local constant-energy surface curvature (hyperbolic regions) and derive a geometric contribution to Fermi velocity that couples to spin; relate spin operator algebra to the exterior algebra of the band's tangent space assuming time-reversal symmetry; formulate spin transport on Fermi surfaces using symplectic geometry for quasi-2D systems and extend to 3D via contact geometry.
specific_terms: exterior algebra of band tangent space

title: Distinguishing Quantum Capacitance Signatures of a Topological Majorana Wire from a Normal Wire Segment
summary: Majorana zero modes (MZMs) are spatially separated, near-zero-energy excitations expected at the ends of a topological superconducting (TS) wire. A quantum-dot interferometer can be used to probe the quantum capacitance of the TS wire, and the location and magnitude of the capacitance resonances provide information about the MZMs, while their magnetic flux dependence probes coherent coupling to the two Majorana modes. It has been recently shown that, a gapless (i.e., $Δ=0$) wire segment can also exhibit flux-dependent quantum capacitance oscillations through Aharonov-Bohm interference and, with suitable tuning, can reproduce a Majorana-like response. Here we show that the two mechanisms can be distinguished experimentally. In the gapless normal wire segment, the two parity-dependent signals originate from separate energy resonances corresponding to the lack of generic zero-energy states. By contrast, in the topological wire, the pair of low energy levels with even and odd parity are nearly degenerate in energy, and therefore, the two parity branches remain within the same broader resonance region in the quantum-dot potential, and persist under independent variations of the dot potential and wire chemical potential. Our results show that the experimentally observed quantum capacitance response is distinguished not by a particular flux trace at one optimized point in parameter space, but by its persistence over a finite range of independently controlled parameters, including the quantum-dot potential. This parameter space stability provides a direct means of ruling out the gapless normal wire segment as the origin of the observed Majorana-like response.

AI.tldr: Quantum-capacitance measurements in a quantum-dot interferometer can distinguish true Majorana zero modes (MZMs) in a topological superconducting (TS) wire from Majorana-like signatures produced by a gapless (Δ=0) normal wire. In the TS case the even/odd parity low-energy levels are nearly degenerate and produce a single, robust resonance region that persists under independent changes of quantum-dot potential and wire chemical potential; in the gapless case the parity signals arise from separate resonances that split under parameter variation. Parameter-space stability of the resonance (not a single tuned flux trace) is the experimental discriminator.
AI.method: Theoretical/phenomenological analysis of quantum-capacitance resonances measured via a quantum-dot interferometer, comparing flux-dependent Aharonov–Bohm interference and parity-resolved energy spectra for (i) a topological superconducting wire hosting MZMs and (ii) a gapless normal wire segment; study of resonance positions, parity-branch degeneracy, and their dependence on quantum-dot potential and wire chemical potential.
